description: Beyond the famous squares, smaller Newar towns around the valley preserve heritage that receives a fraction of the visitors. Kirtipur's hilltop temples, the rain god's village of Bungamati and the oil-pressing village of Khokana, the riverside temples of Panauti, and the hill shrines of Sankhu and Pharping are the focus of efforts to spread visitors toward lesser-known sites.

loreChunks.title: A Goddess and a Guru
loreChunks.text: Pharping, a Newar town on the southern rim of the Kathmandu Valley, is one of the most important sacred sites for both Newar and Tibetan Buddhists. On the hillside above the town stands a temple to Vajrayogini, one of the four Vajrayogini shrines traditionally honoured in the valley. Nearby are caves associated with Padmasambhava, the eighth-century master revered by Tibetans as Guru Rinpoche, who is said to have meditated here and attained realisation before travelling to Tibet. This association has made Pharping a major pilgrimage destination for Tibetan Buddhists, and several monasteries have been built in the area in recent decades. The present Vajrayogini temple is usually attributed to the seventeenth century, though the site's sanctity is older. Pharping also lies on the road to the Hindu shrine of Dakshinkali, linking Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage routes.

loreChunks.title: Temple, Caves and Monasteries
loreChunks.text: The Vajrayogini temple at Pharping is a Newar pagoda with carved struts, gilded elements and a courtyard, set on the hillside above the old town. Around it the hillside holds caves, shrines and newer Tibetan monasteries, creating a layered sacred landscape. The caves associated with Padmasambhava are small and are entered by pilgrims who come to meditate and pray, and the walls around them are covered with prayer flags and butter lamps. The monasteries, built in the Tibetan style with whitewashed walls and gilded roof ornaments, contrast with the Newar temple and the traditional houses of the old town. Paths connect the temple, the caves and the monasteries, and pilgrims often visit them in sequence. Field collectors are asked to document the temple's roof form and carvings, and its relationship with the caves and monasteries on the hillside.

loreChunks.title: The Dakini of Pharping
loreChunks.text: Vajrayogini is a dakini, a female embodiment of enlightened wisdom in Vajrayana Buddhism, typically depicted as red, dancing, holding a curved knife and a skull cup, and wearing ornaments of bone. She represents the transformation of desire and attachment into wisdom. At Pharping her temple belongs to a network of four Vajrayogini shrines that guard the valley, together with those of Sankhu, Guhyeshwari and Bijeshwari. The association with Padmasambhava, whose teachers and consorts included dakinis, strengthens the site's importance for Tibetan Buddhists, who see Pharping as a place where the guru's realisation took place. For Hindus the goddess may be identified with forms of Durga or Kali. The temple's images reflect this layered identity, and pilgrims of several traditions honour the goddess as a powerful source of protection and spiritual insight.

loreChunks.title: Pilgrimage to Pharping
loreChunks.text: Pharping draws pilgrims throughout the year, especially Tibetan Buddhists who come to the caves of Padmasambhava and to the monasteries, and Newar Buddhists and Hindus who honour Vajrayogini. On the tenth day of the lunar month, sacred to Guru Rinpoche, the caves and monasteries are particularly busy, with ritual feasts and prayers. Many Hindu pilgrims pass through Pharping on their way to Dakshinkali, a short distance further south, where animal sacrifices are offered to the goddess Kali, especially on Tuesdays and Saturdays. The combination of Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage gives Pharping a lively and diverse atmosphere. Visitors are welcome at the temple, caves and monasteries, provided they follow the customs of each: walk clockwise, remove shoes where required and ask before photographing. A guide can help visitors navigate the hillside's many sacred sites.

loreChunks.title: Balancing Growth and Heritage
loreChunks.text: Pharping has grown rapidly as a pilgrimage centre, with new monasteries, guesthouses and roads changing the landscape around the old town and the Vajrayogini temple. This growth brings income and support for religious institutions, but it also threatens the setting of the historic temple and the old town. The 2015 earthquake damaged buildings in Pharping, and repairs were carried out by communities and religious organisations. The caves and their surroundings need careful management to cope with large numbers of pilgrims, and butter lamps and incense create risks of smoke damage and fire. Conservation of the temple's carvings and metalwork requires specialist attention. Documentation of the temple, the caves and the changing landscape helps to plan for sustainable pilgrimage. Saalik's field collectors are asked to record the temple and its relationship with the surrounding sacred sites in detail.

audioHook.script: High on the hillside above Pharping, at the southern edge of the valley, a goddess and a guru share a mountain. The temple here belongs to Vajrayogini, a dancing goddess of Tantric wisdom, one of four believed to guard the Kathmandu Valley. Just a short walk away are small caves where, Tibetans believe, Guru Rinpoche meditated in the eighth century and reached realisation before carrying Buddhism over the Himalaya to Tibet. Follow the prayer flags and butter lamps and you will meet Tibetan pilgrims, Newar neighbours and Hindu families on their way to the Kali temple of Dakshinkali further down the road. Three traditions, one hillside. Remove your shoes in the caves and walk clockwise. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Pharping guide lead you from temple to cave.

loreChunks.title: The Tiger God of a Defiant Town
loreChunks.text: Kirtipur, a Newar town on a ridge south-west of Kathmandu, is famous for its resistance to Prithvi Narayan Shah, the Gorkha king who unified Nepal. Its defenders held out against several assaults in the 1760s before the town finally fell in 1767, and chronicles record the harsh punishment that followed, in which many men are said to have had their noses cut off. The temple of Bagh Bhairav, Bhairav in the form of a tiger, stands at the heart of the town, and on its walls hang old swords and shields traditionally said to have belonged to Kirtipur's defenders. The temple is usually attributed to the Malla period, though its exact date has not been confirmed in Saalik's sources. For Kirtipur's residents, Bagh Bhairav is the guardian of the town, and its weapons recall a story of courage that remains central to local identity.

loreChunks.title: A Hilltop Pagoda
loreChunks.text: Bagh Bhairav is a three-tiered pagoda built of brick and timber, with carved struts and a broad facade facing a square in the old town. Its most unusual feature is the collection of swords, shields and other weapons nailed to its walls, which gives the temple a martial character unlike most shrines in the valley. The struts depict deities and attendants, and the roof eaves are hung with bells and ornaments. Kirtipur's position on a ridge means that the temple is surrounded by narrow lanes, steps and traditional Newar houses, many with carved windows. The temple faces a courtyard used for festivals and gatherings. Its architecture follows the Newar pagoda tradition, but its setting and decoration give it a distinctive identity. Field collectors are asked to document the weapons and struts carefully, as they are unique features of this temple.

loreChunks.title: Bhairav as a Tiger
loreChunks.text: Bhairav, the fierce form of Shiva, appears in many guises in the Kathmandu Valley, and at Kirtipur he takes the form of a tiger, bagh in Nepali. A local legend tells of shepherd boys who made a tiger out of clay while grazing their animals and went to find leaves to complete it; when they returned, the clay tiger had come to life and eaten a sheep, revealing the presence of the god. The tiger image inside the temple is honoured as Bhairav, protector of the town. The weapons on the walls reinforce his role as a guardian deity associated with defence and courage. Bhairav's tiger form also links him with the wild forces of nature, which he controls for the benefit of the community. Visitors who look closely at the temple will find images of Bhairav and other deities among the struts and on the facade.

loreChunks.title: Festivals of a Guardian God
loreChunks.text: Bagh Bhairav is worshipped daily by Kirtipur's residents, and major festivals bring the town together in celebration. Animal sacrifices are offered to the god on certain occasions, in keeping with Bhairav worship in the valley. During the town's festivals, processions pass the temple and music fills the square. The temple is also a place where residents seek protection and blessings for important events such as weddings and journeys. Kirtipur's Newar community maintains its rituals through guthis, trusts that organise festivals and care for the temple. The town's location near Tribhuvan University means that students and visitors often come to explore its lanes and temples. Visitors are welcome to observe, but should respect worshippers and not photograph sacrifices. A local guide can explain the history of Kirtipur's resistance and the role of Bagh Bhairav in the town's life.

loreChunks.title: Kirtipur After 2015
loreChunks.text: Kirtipur was affected by the 2015 earthquake, with damage to traditional houses and temples in its old town. Bagh Bhairav required inspection and repair, carried out by local authorities with the community. The town faces pressure from urbanisation, as new buildings replace traditional houses and the ridge is surrounded by the expanding city. Preserving Kirtipur's heritage depends on the commitment of its residents and on support from the municipality and heritage organisations. The weapons on the temple's walls require care, as metal corrodes and wood rots. Documentation of the temple and its weapons, including their arrangement and condition, would support conservation and help to preserve the memory of Kirtipur's history. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the temple from all angles and to record the weapons in detail, with the permission of the temple's custodians.

audioHook.script: Look at the walls of this temple and you will see old swords and shields hanging there. Kirtipur says they belonged to its defenders. In the 1760s this hilltop town held out against the armies of Prithvi Narayan Shah, the king who would unify Nepal, fighting off attack after attack before finally falling in 1767. The punishment was terrible: chronicles say many men had their noses cut off. Inside lives Bagh Bhairav, the god as a tiger. Legend says shepherd boys made a clay tiger here, went off to find leaves, and came back to find it alive and eating a sheep. Ever since, the tiger god has guarded Kirtipur. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Kirtipur guide tell you the story of the siege.

loreChunks.title: Kirtipur's Buddhist Heart
loreChunks.text: Chilanchu Vihar, also called Chilancho, is a Buddhist stupa complex on the southern hill of Kirtipur, dated by inscription to 1515. Kirtipur's population includes a significant Newar Buddhist community, and Chilanchu has long been the centre of their religious life. The central stupa is surrounded by four smaller stupas at the cardinal points, creating a mandala-like arrangement, and the complex is surrounded by monasteries, rest houses and the houses of Buddhist families. Its construction in the early sixteenth century reflects the prosperity of Kirtipur during the Malla period, when the town controlled trade routes and farmland south-west of Kathmandu. Chilanchu offers visitors a quieter alternative to the great stupas of Swayambhu and Boudha, and its setting on a hilltop gives views over the valley toward the Himalaya on clear days.

loreChunks.title: Five Stupas in a Mandala
loreChunks.text: The central stupa of Chilanchu is a hemispherical dome on a base, topped by a harmika and spire, in the classic Newar Buddhist form. Around it four smaller stupas stand at the cardinal directions, reproducing on a small scale the cosmological arrangement of a mandala, with a central axis surrounded by four quarters. Niches in the stupas hold images of Buddhas, and prayer wheels and offerings are found around the base. The complex is enclosed by buildings that serve the Buddhist community, including monasteries known as bahas and bahis. The hilltop setting and the surrounding traditional houses create a peaceful atmosphere. The architecture is modest compared with the great stupas of the valley, but its arrangement and its integration into the life of the town make it a fine example of community Buddhist architecture from the Malla period.

loreChunks.title: The Mandala of the Five Buddhas
loreChunks.text: The arrangement of a central stupa with four smaller stupas reflects the Vajrayana Buddhist mandala of the five Buddhas, each associated with a direction, a colour and an aspect of enlightened wisdom. Vairocana at the centre, Akshobhya in the east, Ratnasambhava in the south, Amitabha in the west and Amoghasiddhi in the north together represent the totality of enlightened mind. The niches of the stupas may hold images of these Buddhas, and devotees circle them clockwise to honour them all. Chilanchu's arrangement thus turns the hilltop into a sacred map of the enlightened universe, like the great stupas of Swayambhu and Boudha but on an intimate scale. For visitors, the complex offers a clear example of how Buddhist cosmology shapes architecture and of how a community expressed its devotion through building.

loreChunks.title: Gunla and Community Worship
loreChunks.text: Chilanchu is the focus of Kirtipur's Buddhist rituals, particularly during Gunla, the sacred month of the Newar Buddhist calendar during the monsoon, when devotees visit stupas and monasteries daily, play traditional music and recite texts. Buddha Jayanti, the festival of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing, also brings the community together. Families perform rituals at the stupa for life-cycle events, and offerings of lamps, flowers and rice are made throughout the year. The monasteries around the stupa host rituals led by Vajracharya priests. Visitors are welcome to walk around the stupa clockwise and observe the community's worship, provided they behave respectfully. Kirtipur's Buddhist heritage is less well known than that of Patan or Kathmandu, and visiting Chilanchu supports the community's efforts to maintain its traditions and its monuments for future generations.

loreChunks.title: Caring for a Community Stupa
loreChunks.text: Chilanchu's conservation depends largely on Kirtipur's Buddhist community, which maintains the stupa and its surroundings through guthis and voluntary contributions. The 2015 earthquake damaged buildings in Kirtipur, including some around the stupa complex, and repairs were carried out with support from local authorities and donors. Whitewashing and repair of the stupas' plaster are periodic tasks, and the images in the niches require care to protect them from weathering and theft. Urban development around Kirtipur's hill threatens the setting of the complex as new buildings rise close to the stupas. Documenting the complex, including the inscription that dates it to 1515, supports conservation and recognition. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph all five stupas, record the inscription and note the condition of the surrounding buildings, with the community's permission.

audioHook.script: On Kirtipur's southern hill, a white stupa stands in the middle of four smaller ones, like a compass pointing to every direction at once. This is Chilanchu, built in 1515 according to its inscription, and it is the heart of Kirtipur's Buddhist community. The five stupas together form a mandala of the five Buddhas, each guarding a direction and a kind of wisdom, a map of the enlightened universe laid out on a hilltop. Walk around clockwise, as the neighbours do, and you will hear prayer wheels turning and perhaps the music of the monsoon month of Gunla. On a clear day the Himalaya rises beyond the city. Which Buddha faces east? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Kirtipur guide introduce you to the town's Buddhist families.

loreChunks.title: A Temple at the Summit
loreChunks.text: At the highest point of Kirtipur's ridge stands the temple of Uma Maheshwar, dedicated to Shiva and Parvati as the divine couple. It is usually attributed to the seventeenth century, though its exact date has not been confirmed in Saalik's sources. Local accounts say the temple originally had four roofs and was reduced to three after damage in the great earthquake of 1934, a claim that field documentation should verify. Its position at the summit made it a landmark visible from much of the valley, and from its plinth visitors enjoy panoramic views over Kathmandu, Patan and, on clear days, the Himalaya. The temple belongs to Kirtipur's rich religious landscape, which includes Hindu temples such as Bagh Bhairav and Buddhist sites such as Chilanchu, reflecting the town's mixed Newar community and its long history as an independent hilltop settlement.

loreChunks.title: Elephants on the Stairs
loreChunks.text: The Uma Maheshwar temple is a three-tiered pagoda raised on a stepped plinth, approached by a stairway guarded by stone elephants. The elephants, described in some accounts as wearing spiked harnesses, give the approach a sense of grandeur. The temple's struts are carved with deities, and the roofs are hung with bells. Its hilltop location exposes it to wind and weather, and its brick and timber construction has been repaired over the centuries. The open space around the temple is used for festivals and gatherings, and benches and walls offer places to rest and enjoy the view. The temple's form follows the classic Newar pagoda, but its setting at the top of a ridge gives it a commanding presence unlike temples in the crowded city squares. Field collectors should photograph the elephants and struts in detail for the record.

loreChunks.title: The Divine Couple on the Hill
loreChunks.text: Uma Maheshwar, Shiva and Parvati together, is one of the most beloved subjects of Newar religious art, representing the harmony of the divine couple on Mount Kailash. The temple's dedication emphasises themes of marital harmony, family well-being and the union of masculine and feminine principles. Images of the couple may appear inside the sanctum or on the struts, accompanied by their sons Ganesh and Kumar and their vehicles, Nandi and the lion. The stone elephants guarding the stairway are royal and protective symbols associated with strength and prosperity. The hilltop setting evokes Kailash itself, the mountain home of the gods, and devotees climbing to the temple may feel that they are ascending toward the divine. For visitors, the temple offers both a religious experience and one of the finest viewpoints anywhere in the Kathmandu Valley.

loreChunks.title: Prayers for Harmony
loreChunks.text: Devotees visit the Uma Maheshwar temple to pray for marital harmony, family well-being and the blessings of the divine couple. Women observe Teej, the festival in which they fast and pray to Parvati for the long life of their husbands or for a good marriage, and Shiva temples are crowded on Mondays and during the month of Shrawan. Maha Shivaratri also brings worshippers. The open space around the temple hosts community gatherings and festivals. Kirtipur's residents climb to the summit for worship, exercise and the view, and the temple is a popular place for photographs, particularly at sunrise and sunset. Visitors are welcome to climb the stairs and enjoy the view, but should respect worshippers and the sanctum. A guide can explain the temple's history and point out landmarks across the valley that are visible from the summit.

loreChunks.title: A Hilltop Temple in a Growing City
loreChunks.text: The Uma Maheshwar temple's hilltop position exposes it to weathering and earthquakes, and its reported damage in 1934 shows its vulnerability. The 2015 earthquake affected Kirtipur, and the temple was inspected and repaired as needed. The stone elephants and carved struts require care to protect them from weathering. Kirtipur's rapid urbanisation threatens the setting of the temple, as new buildings encroach on the ridge and block views. Preserving the temple's surroundings is as important as conserving the building itself. Kirtipur Municipality and local guthis share responsibility for the temple, supported by heritage authorities. Documentation of the temple's current state, including evidence for its original fourth roof, would help clarify its history. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the temple, its elephants and its views, and to record any inscriptions found on site.

audioHook.script: Climb to the very top of Kirtipur's ridge, past the stone elephants guarding the stairway, and turn around. The whole valley spreads out below you: Kathmandu, Patan and, on a clear day, the white line of the Himalaya. You are at the temple of Uma Maheshwar, Shiva and Parvati together, the divine couple whose mountain home is Kailash, and this hilltop feels like a small Kailash of its own. People in Kirtipur say the temple once had four roofs until the great earthquake of 1934 took one away; our field team is checking that story. Couples come here to pray for a happy marriage, and everyone comes for the sunset. Can you find Swayambhu's stupa from here? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide point out the valley's landmarks.

loreChunks.title: The Goddess of the Oil Village
loreChunks.text: Khokana is a traditional Newar village south of Patan, known for its mustard oil, pressed for generations in wooden presses, and for its well-preserved village life. At its centre stands the temple of Rudrayani, the village's protective goddess, one of the mother goddesses who guard Newar settlements. The temple's date has not been established in Saalik's sources, and its history is preserved in local tradition and in the rituals of the community. Khokana's goddesses are honoured during the Shikali festival, a major annual celebration in which the village holds processions, music and rituals. The village was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquake, and its recovery has tested the community's determination to preserve its heritage. Khokana's traditional character, so close to the growing city, makes it a valuable example of rural Newar culture and of the pressures that culture now faces.

loreChunks.title: A Village Pagoda
loreChunks.text: Rudrayani's temple is a pagoda in the Newar style, with brick walls, carved wooden struts and doors, and tiled roofs, standing in the village's central area. The temple is surrounded by traditional houses with carved windows, many of them damaged in 2015 and since rebuilt or repaired. Khokana's village plan, with its narrow lanes, courtyards and open spaces, is typical of Newar settlements, and the temple provides a focal point for community life. The village's oil presses, some of which still operate using traditional methods, are housed in buildings around the village and can be visited. The architecture of Khokana shows how a rural community organised its sacred and productive spaces together. Field collectors are asked to document the temple's roof tiers, struts and doors, as well as its relationship to the surrounding village and its oil presses.

loreChunks.title: Rudrayani, Mother Protector
loreChunks.text: Rudrayani is understood as a form of the mother goddess associated with Rudra, a fierce form of Shiva, and she is honoured as the protector of Khokana and its people. In the Newar tradition, towns and villages are protected by a circle of mother goddesses, the Ashta Matrika, whose shrines stand at the edges and centres of settlements. Rudrayani's image is honoured with offerings and rituals, and on certain occasions with animal sacrifices, in keeping with goddess worship in the valley. Her temple's struts may depict goddesses and attendant figures. For villagers the goddess is a source of protection against disease, misfortune and disaster, and her worship binds the community together. Visitors interested in Newar religion will find in Khokana a clear example of how the mother goddesses structure the sacred life of a settlement from its centre to its edges.

loreChunks.title: Shikali Jatra and Village Life
loreChunks.text: Khokana's most important festival is the Shikali Jatra, held in the autumn around the time of Dashain, when the village honours its goddesses with processions, masked dances, music and rituals over several days. The festival draws residents who have moved away back to the village and attracts visitors from nearby towns. Throughout the year villagers worship Rudrayani daily, and the temple is a focus of life-cycle rituals. Khokana's agricultural calendar, with its rice planting and harvest, is also marked by rituals. The village's mustard oil tradition is part of its identity, and visitors can see oil being pressed in some workshops. Visitors are welcome to explore the village and observe its life, but should respect residents' privacy and ask permission before photographing people or entering courtyards. A local guide can explain the festivals and the village's long history.

loreChunks.title: Rebuilding a Traditional Village
loreChunks.text: Khokana suffered heavy damage in the 2015 earthquake, with many traditional houses destroyed and others badly cracked, and the temple of Rudrayani was also affected. Reconstruction has been a long process involving the community, local authorities and heritage organisations, with debates about whether to rebuild in traditional styles or with modern materials. Some programmes supported traditional reconstruction, helping to preserve the village's character. Khokana also faces pressure from infrastructure projects, including a planned expressway that many residents have opposed because of its impact on their land and heritage. The village's future depends on balancing development with the preservation of its traditional life, crafts and festivals. Documentation of the temple and village, including oral histories, contributes to this effort, and Saalik's field collectors are asked to record both with the community's consent.

audioHook.script: Smell the air in Khokana and you may catch the sharp scent of mustard oil. For generations this village has pressed oil in heavy wooden presses, and some still work today. At the centre of the village stands the temple of Rudrayani, the mother goddess who protects Khokana. Every autumn, during the Shikali festival, villagers who have moved to the city come home to dance, play music and honour their goddesses for days. In 2015 the earthquake shattered much of Khokana, and its people have been rebuilding their homes and temples ever since, while fighting to keep their land and way of life as the city creeps closer. Want to see an oil press in action? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Khokana guide welcome you into village life.

loreChunks.title: Ganesh Who Makes Things Happen
loreChunks.text: On a wooded hilltop between the villages of Bungamati and Khokana stands the shrine of Karya Binayak, a form of Ganesh whose name means 'the Ganesh who accomplishes tasks'. Karya Binayak is an important Ganesh shrine of the southern valley, and devotees come here to pray for the success of their undertakings, from business ventures to examinations and journeys. The image is not a carved statue but a natural rock, revered as a self-manifested form of the god. The shrine's date has not been established in Saalik's sources, and its history is preserved mainly in local tradition. Its location between two traditional Newar villages and above the fields of the southern valley makes it a peaceful place to visit, and the walk between Bungamati, Karya Binayak and Khokana is one of the most rewarding short walks near Kathmandu.

loreChunks.title: A Hilltop Shrine Among Trees
loreChunks.text: The shrine of Karya Binayak is modest in form, a small structure sheltering the natural stone image, surrounded by trees and smaller shrines on the hilltop. Its simplicity reflects the nature of the deity's manifestation: the holiness lies in the rock itself rather than in elaborate architecture. A small courtyard and platforms around the shrine provide space for worshippers and rituals, and bells hang at the entrance to be rung by devotees as they arrive. The surrounding woodland offers shade and quiet, and the hilltop gives views over the fields toward Bungamati, Khokana and the southern hills. Paths lead down to both villages, making the shrine part of a walking circuit. Field collectors are asked to record the shrine's structure, the natural rock image and the surrounding shrines, as well as the paths that link the hilltop with the villages below it.

loreChunks.title: The Self-Manifested Ganesh
loreChunks.text: Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati, is the remover of obstacles and the lord of beginnings, worshipped before any new undertaking. At Karya Binayak the god is manifested in a natural rock, svayambhu or self-arisen, rather than in a sculpted image, and devotees see in its form the presence of Ganesh. The rock is covered with red powder and offerings, and a small figure of a shrew, Ganesh's vehicle, may be present. Natural stone images of deities are common in the Kathmandu Valley, where rocks, springs and trees are often regarded as sacred manifestations. The valley's best-known Ganesh shrines include Surya Binayak near Bhaktapur, Jal Binayak at Chobhar and Ashok Binayak beside Kasthamandap, and Karya Binayak holds a special place in the southern valley. Praying here before an important task is believed to remove obstacles.

loreChunks.title: Prayers Before Undertakings
loreChunks.text: Devotees visit Karya Binayak to pray before beginning important tasks, offering flowers, rice, red powder, sweets and coins. Tuesdays, sacred to Ganesh in Nepal, bring additional worshippers, and Ganesh Chaturthi, the god's festival, is a major occasion. Students pray for success in examinations, business owners for profitable ventures and families for successful weddings or new homes. The shrine is also visited by people from Bungamati and Khokana as part of their village festivals. Visitors who walk between the two villages often stop at the shrine, and its quiet atmosphere contrasts with the busy temples of the city. Visitors are welcome to observe and to make an offering if they wish, but should respect the shrine and its worshippers. A guide can explain the significance of the natural stone image and the rituals performed at this peaceful hilltop shrine.

loreChunks.title: Protecting a Sacred Grove
loreChunks.text: Karya Binayak's hilltop setting, with its trees and shrines, is as important as the shrine itself, and protecting the woodland from encroachment and degradation is essential. The 2015 earthquake damaged buildings in Bungamati and Khokana, and the shrine and its surroundings were inspected for damage. Urban expansion from Lalitpur threatens the rural landscape between the villages, as new roads and buildings spread into the fields. Preserving the walking routes between Bungamati, Karya Binayak and Khokana, and the views from the hilltop, requires coordination between the municipality and the communities. The shrine's maintenance depends on local guthis and devotees. Documentation of the shrine, its natural image and its setting helps to record this heritage and support planning. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the shrine, the grove and the views, and to map the connecting paths.

audioHook.script: On a wooded hill between the villages of Bungamati and Khokana sits a small shrine with a big job. This is Karya Binayak, the Ganesh who makes things happen. The god here was not carved by any sculptor: he is a natural rock, smeared with red powder, believed to have revealed himself in stone. People climb up before exams, business deals, weddings and journeys, ring the bell, leave a sweet and ask Ganesh to clear the obstacles from their path. On Tuesdays, Ganesh's day, the hilltop gets busy. The walk from Khokana up to this shrine and down to Bungamati is one of the loveliest short walks in the valley. What are you hoping Ganesh will help you with? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide walk the village trail with you.

loreChunks.title: Home of the Rain God
loreChunks.text: Bungamati, a Newar village south of Patan, is considered the birthplace and second home of Rato Machhindranath, the 'Red Matsyendranath', worshipped by Newar Buddhists as Bunga Dyah or Karunamaya, the compassionate Avalokiteshvara, and by Hindus as Matsyendranath. Legend tells that during a terrible drought, caused when the yogi Gorakhnath sat in meditation on the rain-giving serpents, the king and priests travelled to Kamarupa in Assam to bring Matsyendranath, Gorakhnath's guru, to the valley. When the guru arrived, Gorakhnath rose to greet him, releasing the serpents, and the rains returned. The deity is said to have been installed at Bungamati, and he spends part of each year here and part in Patan. His great chariot festival is the longest in the valley. Bungamati's temple, in the village square, was destroyed in 2015 and has been rebuilt by the community.

loreChunks.title: A Shikhara in a Village Square
loreChunks.text: Rato Machhindranath's temple at Bungamati is a shikhara, a tall tapering tower, standing in the centre of the village's main square. The square is surrounded by traditional Newar houses, rest houses and shrines, creating an ensemble that had changed little in centuries before the damage of 2015. The temple's whitewashed tower is topped by a gilded finial, and its doorway is framed by carved and metal decoration. The square provides space for festivals and for the community's daily life, with residents gathering on platforms and children playing. Bungamati's architecture, with its brick houses, carved windows and narrow lanes, makes it one of the best-preserved traditional villages in the valley, and it is known for its woodcarvers, whose workshops line the streets. The rebuilding of the temple after 2015 has been a major effort for the whole community.

loreChunks.title: The Compassionate Red God
loreChunks.text: Rato Machhindranath's image is painted red, the colour associated with compassion and with the deity's role as giver of rain and fertility. For Newar Buddhists he is Karunamaya, 'full of compassion', a form of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, who vowed to save all beings from suffering. For Hindus he is Matsyendranath, the great yogi and guru of Gorakhnath. This dual identity makes him one of the clearest examples of the valley's shared Hindu-Buddhist religion. The image is small, with a red face and painted features, and it is dressed and adorned by priests. Its annual bathing ceremony and chariot festival are among the most important rituals of the valley. The deity's role as rain-bringer connects him with the agricultural cycle and the monsoon, on which the valley's rice harvest depends, making his worship a matter of survival as well as devotion.

loreChunks.title: The Longest Chariot Festival
loreChunks.text: Rato Machhindranath's chariot festival, held each spring before the monsoon, is the longest and one of the most important festivals in the Kathmandu Valley. A towering chariot, built anew each year from timber and bamboo following strict traditional rules, carries the deity through the streets of Patan over several weeks, pulled by crowds of devotees. The festival culminates in the Bhoto Jatra, when a jewelled vest is displayed to the public, an event traditionally attended by the head of state. Every twelve years the chariot journey begins in Bungamati, with the chariot pulled all the way from the village to Patan, a monumental undertaking. In Bungamati, the deity's residence for part of the year is marked by rituals and community celebrations. Visitors who witness the festival see one of the greatest living expressions of Newar culture anywhere in Nepal.

loreChunks.title: Rebuilding After 2015
loreChunks.text: The 2015 earthquake devastated Bungamati, destroying the Rato Machhindranath temple and many traditional houses. The collapse of the temple was a heavy blow to the community, and its reconstruction became a priority. Rebuilding has been carried out with the involvement of the Department of Archaeology, local authorities and the community, using traditional materials and techniques with structural improvements. The village's traditional houses were also rebuilt, some with support from heritage programmes that encouraged traditional designs, though concrete construction has also spread. Bungamati's woodcarvers played an important role in the recovery, providing carved elements for rebuilt buildings. The village's heritage depends on the continuation of its festivals, crafts and community life as well as on its buildings. Visitors can support the recovery by visiting, buying carvings from local workshops and respecting the community's rituals.

audioHook.script: In the middle of this village square stands the temple of Rato Machhindranath, the red god of rain. Legend says a terrible drought once struck the valley because the yogi Gorakhnath was sitting in meditation on the rain serpents. So the king fetched Gorakhnath's own teacher, Matsyendranath, from distant Assam. When the guru arrived, Gorakhnath stood up to bow, the serpents slipped free and the rains poured down. Buddhists here call the god Karunamaya, the compassionate one, and every spring his towering chariot rolls through Patan in the longest festival in the valley. Every twelve years it begins right here in Bungamati. The 2015 earthquake brought this temple down, and the village has rebuilt it. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Bungamati guide show you the woodcarvers' lanes.

loreChunks.title: One of Nepal's Oldest Pagodas
loreChunks.text: Indreshwar Mahadev, in the town of Panauti south-east of the Kathmandu Valley, is often described as one of the oldest and largest pagoda temples in Nepal, traditionally dated to 1294. The temple is dedicated to Shiva as Indreshwar, 'lord of Indra', a name linked to the legend of the god Indra's penance at this site. Panauti was an important town on trade routes and stands at the confluence of the Roshi and Punyamati rivers, with a third, invisible river, the Lilavati, said to join them, making the confluence sacred. The town has a rich heritage of temples, ghats and traditional houses. Indreshwar's early date makes it a valuable witness to the architecture of the early Malla period, though the temple has been repaired many times, including after the 1988 earthquake. Panauti is less visited than the valley's cities, which rewards those who make the journey.

loreChunks.title: Struts from the Early Malla Age
loreChunks.text: Indreshwar Mahadev is a large three-tiered pagoda raised on a plinth, standing in a spacious courtyard surrounded by smaller shrines and buildings. Its roof struts are celebrated as some of the oldest surviving examples of Newar woodcarving, depicting deities and, at their lower ends, erotic scenes in a style that differs from the more elaborate carvings of later centuries. The temple's proportions are broad and massive, giving it an imposing presence. The courtyard includes shrines to other deities and a Nandi facing the temple. Panauti's old town, with its brick houses and narrow lanes, surrounds the temple complex, and the riverside ghats lie nearby. The temple has been studied by scholars interested in the development of the Newar pagoda, and its struts are a key reference for understanding early Malla carving styles and how they evolved.

loreChunks.title: Indra's Penance
loreChunks.text: The legend of Indreshwar tells that Indra, king of the gods, came to this place to perform penance after committing an offence, and that Shiva, pleased with his devotion, granted him forgiveness and manifested here as a lingam. The temple's name honours this story, linking the god of rain and the heavens with Shiva, the lord of transformation. The lingam inside the sanctum is the focus of worship, and Nandi faces it from the courtyard. The struts depict various deities, including forms of Shiva and the goddess, and the erotic scenes at their lower ends express the Tantric concept of union. Panauti's sacred geography, with its confluence of three rivers, adds to the temple's significance, since confluences are considered especially powerful places for worship and purification. The temple and the confluence together form Panauti's sacred core.

loreChunks.title: Panauti Jatra and Makar Mela
loreChunks.text: Panauti's festival calendar centres on the Panauti Jatra, a chariot festival held each year in late spring, when the town's deities, including Indreshwar Mahadev and the goddess Brahmayani, are carried in chariots through the streets. The festival is one of the most important in the region, drawing residents and visitors from surrounding villages. Every twelve years Panauti hosts the Makar Mela, a great bathing festival at the river confluence, when pilgrims come to bathe in the sacred waters, an occasion often compared on a smaller scale with India's Kumbh Mela. Throughout the year the temple receives daily worship, and Shiva's festivals, such as Maha Shivaratri, bring crowds. Visitors are welcome to observe, but should respect the sanctum and the worshippers. A local guide can explain the festivals and the legends of the confluence in detail.

loreChunks.title: Restoring Panauti's Treasure
loreChunks.text: Indreshwar Mahadev has been repaired many times over its long history, including after the earthquake of 1988, which damaged temples in the region, and after the 2015 earthquake. Restoration work has involved national heritage authorities and international partners, and the temple's ancient struts have received particular attention, since they are among the most important surviving examples of early Newar carving. Panauti's old town has also benefited from conservation programmes aimed at preserving its traditional houses and streets, and the town has promoted community-based tourism, including homestays, to support its heritage. The pressures of modernisation and new construction remain a challenge. Documentation of the temple's struts, in particular, supports both conservation and scholarly research. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the struts systematically and to record the temple's condition, with permission from its custodians.

audioHook.script: Panauti is a small town about thirty kilometres from Kathmandu, and at its heart stands one of the oldest pagoda temples in Nepal: Indreshwar Mahadev, traditionally dated to 1294. Look up at the roof struts. They are among the oldest surviving Newar woodcarvings anywhere, made long before the famous temples of the Durbar Squares. Legend says Indra, king of the gods, came here to do penance, and Shiva forgave him and appeared as the lingam inside. Just beyond the temple, two rivers meet, and tradition says a third, invisible river joins them, making the confluence holy. Every twelve years pilgrims crowd in to bathe there during the Makar Mela. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Panauti guide or homestay host show you their town.

loreChunks.title: Panauti's Protective Goddess
loreChunks.text: Brahmayani is the tutelary goddess of Panauti, and her temple stands near the confluence of the rivers that make the town sacred. She is one of the Ashta Matrika, the eight mother goddesses who protect Newar towns, and is associated with Brahma, the creator god. In Panauti she holds a special place as the town's guardian, and her chariot is one of the central features of the annual Panauti Jatra. The temple's date has not been established in Saalik's sources, and it is attributed to the Malla period by tradition. Panauti's sacred landscape, with Indreshwar Mahadev in the town and Brahmayani by the river, creates a pairing of god and goddess that structures the town's religious life. For visitors, the temple offers a glimpse of how Newar towns honour the mother goddesses who are believed to keep them safe from harm.

loreChunks.title: A Riverside Temple
loreChunks.text: Brahmayani's temple is a Newar pagoda with brick walls, carved struts and tiled roofs, set near the riverbank where the Punyamati and Roshi rivers meet. Its riverside setting connects it with the ghats and with the rituals of bathing and purification performed at the confluence. Steps lead from the temple area to the water, and smaller shrines and rest houses stand nearby. The temple's carved struts depict goddesses and attendant figures, and its doors and windows are decorated in the Newar tradition. Its roof form and carvings should be documented in the field, as published descriptions are limited. The surrounding landscape of rivers, fields and hills gives the temple a peaceful setting, and the view across the river toward the old town of Panauti, with Indreshwar's roofs rising above, is one of the most attractive views anywhere in the area.

loreChunks.title: The Mother on a Swan
loreChunks.text: Brahmayani, also called Brahmani, is the shakti or female energy of Brahma, and she is often depicted riding a swan, Brahma's vehicle, and holding attributes associated with him, such as a water pot and a rosary. As one of the Ashta Matrika, she is part of the circle of mother goddesses who protect Newar settlements from misfortune and disease. Each mother goddess has her own direction, attributes and vehicle, and together they form a protective mandala around the town. In Panauti, Brahmayani is the most important of these goddesses, and her worship is central to the town's festivals. Her image is honoured with offerings and rituals, sometimes including animal sacrifices. For devotees she is a powerful and compassionate protector, and her presence beside the sacred confluence adds to the sanctity that the whole town draws from its rivers.

loreChunks.title: The Goddess's Chariot
loreChunks.text: During the Panauti Jatra, held each year in late spring, Brahmayani's image is placed on a chariot and pulled through the streets of Panauti along with the chariots of other deities, including Indreshwar Mahadev. The festival lasts several days and includes rituals, music and celebrations, and the meeting of the deities' chariots is a highlight. The festival reflects the town's sacred geography, linking the goddess by the river with the god in the town centre. Throughout the year Brahmayani is worshipped by residents, especially women and families seeking her protection, and during Dashain her temple receives special rituals. Visitors who come to Panauti during the Jatra can witness one of the most vibrant festivals outside the valley's cities. Visitors should respect the rituals, avoid photographing sacrifices and follow the guidance of local organisers during the festival.

loreChunks.title: Rivers, Floods and Earthquakes
loreChunks.text: Brahmayani's riverside location exposes it to flooding during the monsoon, as well as to the earthquakes that have affected Panauti over the centuries. The 1988 and 2015 earthquakes damaged temples in the area, and repairs were carried out by local authorities with heritage organisations. The health of the rivers at the confluence is also important for the temple's setting and for the rituals performed there, and pollution and changes in water flow are concerns. Panauti's community-based tourism initiatives, including homestays, help to support heritage conservation by bringing income to the town. Documentation of the temple's structure, carvings and riverside setting would help to plan conservation and to understand its history. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the temple, record its roof form and carvings, and note its relationship with the ghats and the confluence.

audioHook.script: Cross toward the river in Panauti and you reach the temple of Brahmayani, the mother goddess who protects this town. Look for her vehicle, a swan, borrowed from Brahma the creator, whose female power she embodies. Her temple stands near the confluence where two visible rivers and, tradition says, one invisible river meet, making this one of the holiest spots in the region. Every spring, during the Panauti Jatra, Brahmayani rides through town on a chariot to meet Indreshwar, Shiva's ancient temple in the centre, and the whole town comes out to celebrate. Look back across the water and you can see Indreshwar's roofs rising over the old town. Where does the invisible river come from? loreChunks.title: The Goddess Above Sankhu
loreChunks.text: On a forested hillside above the old Newar town of Sankhu, in the north-eastern corner of the Kathmandu Valley, stands the temple complex of Bajrayogini, one of the four Vajrayogini shrines traditionally honoured in the valley. Sankhu, known in Newar as Sakwa, was an important town on the old trade route between Kathmandu and Tibet, and its goddess was revered by traders and pilgrims. The present three-tiered temple is usually attributed to the seventeenth century, with some accounts associating it with King Pratap Malla, though the site's sanctity is much older. Vajrayogini, a Tantric goddess, is honoured by both Buddhists and Hindus, the latter often identifying her with Ugratara or other forms of the goddess. The complex includes several shrines, rest houses and a stupa, and its forest setting makes it one of the most atmospheric sacred sites in the valley.

loreChunks.title: A Temple in the Forest
loreChunks.text: The Bajrayogini complex is reached by a stone stairway that climbs through the forest from Sankhu, passing shrines and resting places along the way. At the top, a courtyard holds the main three-tiered pagoda, with gilded roofs, carved struts and gilded toranas, along with a second temple, smaller shrines and a stupa. The buildings around the courtyard include rest houses for pilgrims and quarters for priests. The temple's carvings and metalwork are of high quality, reflecting the patronage of kings and merchants. The forest setting, with tall trees and birdsong, contrasts with the urban temples of the valley's cities and creates a sense of remoteness. From the complex, paths lead further into the hills, and the views over the valley are striking on clear days. Field collectors should document the complex's layout and each of its several buildings in turn.

loreChunks.title: Vajrayogini, Tantric Wisdom
loreChunks.text: Vajrayogini is a Tantric deity in Vajrayana Buddhism, a dakini or female embodiment of enlightened wisdom, often depicted dancing, red in colour, holding a skull cup and a curved knife. She represents the transformation of passion into wisdom and is a central figure in certain Tantric practices. In the Kathmandu Valley, four Vajrayogini temples, at Sankhu, Pharping, Guhyeshwari and Bijeshwari, are traditionally associated with the directions and form a protective network. Hindus honour the goddess in her Ugratara form, emphasising her fierce, protective power. The image inside the Sankhu temple is not publicly displayed in full, in keeping with the secrecy of Tantric deities, and the temple's struts and toranas carry images of the goddess and her attendants. For visitors, the shrine offers insight into the esoteric dimensions of the valley's shared Buddhist and Hindu religion.

loreChunks.title: Pilgrims, Festivals and Tantric Worship
loreChunks.text: Bajrayogini is visited by pilgrims from across the valley, and the climb through the forest is part of the devotional experience. Sankhu's main festival, held in spring, includes a procession in which the goddess is carried down from the hilltop to the town, bringing the community together in celebration, with Buddhists and Hindus both taking part. Throughout the year Tantric rituals are performed by priests, some of them restricted to initiates. Sankhu is also famous during the winter month of Magh, when devotees observe the Swasthani vrata and gather along the Salinadi river near the town. Visitors are welcome at the complex, but should respect the sanctum and any restricted rituals. A guide from Sankhu can explain the festivals, the town's history on the Tibet trade route and the shrine's place in the sacred geography of the Kathmandu Valley.

loreChunks.title: Sankhu After the Earthquake
loreChunks.text: Sankhu was one of the most severely damaged towns in the 2015 earthquake, with much of its old town destroyed and many lives lost. The Bajrayogini complex on the hillside was also damaged, and its restoration has been part of the long recovery of the area. Reconstruction in Sankhu's old town has been slow and challenging, with debates about traditional and modern building styles. The forest around the temple complex needs protection from encroachment and degradation, and the stairway and paths require maintenance. The temple's gilded metalwork and carved struts need specialist conservation. Documenting the complex and the town's recovery is important for understanding how heritage can be rebuilt after disaster. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the complex and its approaches, record its current condition and gather the community's own accounts of its history and recovery since 2015.

audioHook.script: Climb the stone stairway through the forest above Sankhu, and the sound of the town falls away until you hear only birds and temple bells. At the top waits Bajrayogini, a Tantric goddess of wisdom honoured by Buddhists and Hindus alike, in a three-roofed temple glinting with gold among the trees. Sankhu once stood on the road to Tibet, and traders stopped here to ask the goddess for safe passage. She is one of four Vajrayoginis believed to guard the valley, together with Pharping, Guhyeshwari and Bijeshwari. In 2015 the earthquake devastated Sankhu, and its people are still rebuilding. Every spring the goddess is carried down the hill to her town for a festival. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Sankhu guide walk the forest stairway with you.

loreChunks.title: Kali of the South
loreChunks.text: Dakshinkali, 'Kali of the south', is one of the most important goddess shrines in Nepal, set in a forested ravine at the meeting of two streams below the town of Pharping, on the southern edge of the Kathmandu Valley. Tradition associates its establishment with King Pratap Malla of Kathmandu in the seventeenth century, who is said to have been instructed by the goddess in a dream to build her shrine here, though the site may have been sacred earlier and the attribution should be confirmed. Kali is the fierce form of the goddess who destroys demons and protects her devotees, and her worship at Dakshinkali is famous for its animal sacrifices. The shrine draws large crowds from Kathmandu and beyond, especially on its special days, and the road from the city to Dakshinkali passes through Pharping, linking Hindu and Buddhist pilgrimage in one journey.

loreChunks.title: A Shrine at the Bottom of a Ravine
loreChunks.text: Dakshinkali's setting is its most striking architectural feature. A long stairway descends from the road into a wooded ravine, where the shrine stands at the confluence of two streams, open to the sky rather than enclosed in a tiered temple. The sanctum is covered by a gilded canopy, and around it are platforms for ritual, smaller shrines and enclosures where sacrifices are performed. The approach is lined with stalls selling offerings, flowers, coconuts and sweets. On busy days, devotees queue along railings on the stairway for their turn to reach the goddess. Picnic areas in the surrounding forest are used by families after their worship. The arrangement, with its descent into a green ravine, gives the visit a sense of journey into the goddess's domain. Field collectors are asked to document the stairway, the canopy and the shrine's relationship to the streams.

loreChunks.title: The Fierce Mother
loreChunks.text: Kali is the fierce, dark form of the great goddess, often depicted with a garland of skulls, a protruding tongue and weapons in her many hands, standing over the body of Shiva. At Dakshinkali the goddess is represented by a black stone image within the sanctum, beneath the gilded canopy. Kali embodies time, death and transformation, and she destroys demons that threaten the world and her devotees. Her fierceness is understood as protective: she is a mother who fights for her children. Sacrifices offered to her are interpreted in Hindu tradition as offerings of life force, returning to the goddess the energy she sustains. The confluence of streams at the shrine adds to its power, since meeting waters are sacred throughout the valley. For many visitors the shrine's intensity is challenging, but it reveals an important dimension of Nepali goddess worship.

loreChunks.title: Tuesdays, Saturdays and Dashain
loreChunks.text: Dakshinkali is busiest on Tuesdays and Saturdays, the days traditionally favoured for worshipping the goddess here, when thousands of devotees come to make offerings and, in many cases, to sacrifice animals, usually male goats and chickens, through the shrine's priests and attendants. During Dashain, the great autumn festival of Durga, the crowds are enormous. After the sacrifice, families often cook and share the meat as a blessed feast in the picnic areas around the ravine, turning the visit into a family outing that combines devotion with celebration. Vegetarian offerings of flowers, fruit and sweets are also common. Visitors are welcome to observe from the stairway and surrounding areas, but should be prepared for the sight of sacrifices, should not photograph them and should respect worshippers in the queue. A guide can explain the rituals and their meaning with sensitivity.

loreChunks.title: Managing Crowds in a Ravine
loreChunks.text: Dakshinkali's popularity creates significant management challenges. The ravine setting concentrates crowds on narrow stairways, and safety measures such as railings and queue management are essential on busy days. Waste from offerings and picnics, along with the by-products of sacrifices, must be managed to protect the streams and forest. The 2015 earthquake affected buildings in the area, and structures at the shrine were inspected and repaired. The gilded canopy and the shrine's metalwork require periodic conservation. Debates about animal sacrifice, including campaigns by animal welfare groups, form part of the shrine's contemporary context, and the community's practices continue to evolve. Documentation of the shrine and its setting supports planning for safety and environmental protection. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the stairway, canopy and ravine on a quieter weekday, without photographing sacrifices or identifiable worshippers.

audioHook.script: Follow the long stairway down into this forested ravine, and the air grows cooler as two streams meet below you. Here, at the bottom, is Dakshinkali, Kali of the south, one of the most powerful goddess shrines in Nepal. Tradition says King Pratap Malla built it after the goddess appeared to him in a dream. Kali is the fierce mother who destroys demons to protect her children, and on Tuesdays and Saturdays thousands of devotees queue here to make offerings, many of them animal sacrifices, before sharing a family feast in the forest above. It can be an intense experience, so be ready, keep your camera down near the shrine, and respect those in the queue. What does sacrifice mean to Kali's devotees? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide explain the goddess with care.

loreChunks.title: Ganesh at the Valley's Outlet
loreChunks.text: Jal Binayak, 'Ganesh of the water', stands on the bank of the Bagmati river at Chobhar, where the river leaves the Kathmandu Valley through a narrow gorge. The temple is traditionally dated to 1602, though this should be confirmed from inscriptions, and it is often counted among the most important Ganesh shrines in the valley. Its location gives it special significance: the Chobhar gorge is identified in the Swayambhu Purana as the cut made by Manjushri's sword to drain the primordial lake that once filled the valley, and geologists agree that the valley was indeed once a lake. Jal Binayak thus guards the place where, in legend, the waters rushed out and the valley was born. The temple lies between Kirtipur and the villages of Khokana and Bungamati, making it a natural stop on a journey through the southern valley's heritage towns.

loreChunks.title: A Pagoda Above the Gorge
loreChunks.text: Jal Binayak is a three-tiered pagoda with carved struts, wooden doors and gilded elements, raised on a plinth near the river. Its roof struts are carved with deities, and the temple is surrounded by a small courtyard and shrines. The setting is dramatic: the Bagmati flows through the rocky Chobhar gorge just below, crossed by a historic iron suspension bridge, and cliffs rise on either side. The temple's form follows the classic Newar pagoda tradition, but its riverside setting, away from dense urban squares, gives it a quieter, more natural atmosphere. Nearby, the Chobhar caves and the gorge itself attract visitors interested in geology as well as religion. Field collectors are asked to document the temple's struts and roofs, its relationship with the gorge and the river, and any inscriptions that could confirm the date of its construction.

loreChunks.title: The Rock That Is Ganesh
loreChunks.text: As at several of the valley's important Ganesh shrines, the god at Jal Binayak is worshipped in the form of a natural rock rather than a carved statue, understood as a self-manifested form of the elephant-headed remover of obstacles. The rock is covered in red powder and offerings, and Ganesh's vehicle, the shrew, is represented nearby. The temple's struts depict Ganesh and other deities in the Newar style. The name 'Ganesh of the water' links the god with the river and with the legend of the draining of the lake, so that Ganesh, lord of beginnings, presides over the beginning of the valley itself. For devotees, worship here ensures that obstacles are removed and that new undertakings succeed. For visitors, the shrine offers a link between the valley's founding myth, its geology and the everyday devotion of people who come to pray at the river's edge.

loreChunks.title: Tuesday Prayers by the River
loreChunks.text: Jal Binayak receives regular worship, especially on Tuesdays, sacred to Ganesh in Nepal, when devotees from nearby towns and from Kathmandu come to pray. Ganesh Chaturthi, the god's festival, brings larger crowds. Devotees offer red powder, flowers, sweets and coins, and some bring new vehicles or prepare for weddings and journeys with a visit to the temple. The riverside setting makes the shrine a pleasant place to linger, and many visitors combine worship with a walk across the old iron bridge over the gorge or a visit to the nearby caves. The temple is part of the circuit of the southern valley's heritage sites, linking Kirtipur with Khokana and Bungamati. Visitors are welcome to observe and to make offerings, but should respect worshippers and the sanctum. A guide can tell the full legend of Manjushri and the lake at the gorge itself.

loreChunks.title: A Sacred River in Trouble
loreChunks.text: Jal Binayak's setting beside the Bagmati exposes it to the river's problems: pollution from the city upstream, floods during the monsoon and changes to the riverbank caused by development and quarrying. The water flowing through the gorge carries much of the valley's waste, and clean-up campaigns along the Bagmati aim to improve conditions here as elsewhere. The 2015 earthquake affected buildings in the area, and the temple was inspected and repaired as needed. Its carved struts and gilded elements require periodic conservation, and the plinth must be protected from flood damage. Preserving the gorge landscape, including its cliffs, caves and historic bridge, is as important as conserving the temple itself. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the temple, the gorge and the river together, recording their condition and documenting the relationship between the shrine and the landscape of its legend.

audioHook.script: Stand by this three-roofed temple and listen to the Bagmati rushing through the narrow gorge below. Legend says this is exactly where Manjushri raised his sword and cut the hills, letting the ancient lake drain away so that the Kathmandu Valley could be born. Geologists agree the valley really was once a lake. Guarding the gorge is Jal Binayak, the Ganesh of the water, worshipped here as a natural rock smeared with red powder, traditionally since 1602. Ganesh is the lord of beginnings, so who better to watch over the beginning of the whole valley? On Tuesdays, Ganesh's day, families come to pray before new ventures. Walk out onto the old iron bridge for the best view of the gorge. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide tell you the full legend of the lake.

loreChunks.title: Where Three Rivers Meet
loreChunks.text: Tribeni Ghat in Panauti marks the confluence of the Roshi and Punyamati rivers, joined, according to tradition, by a third, invisible river called the Lilavati, so that the place is a tribeni, a meeting of three rivers. Confluences are especially sacred in Hindu tradition, and Panauti's has been honoured for centuries with ghats, shrines, rest houses and cremation platforms built by successive generations of the town's residents and patrons. Saalik's sources do not record precise dates for the ghat's individual structures, which appear to belong to the Malla and later periods. The confluence is the sacred heart of Panauti, linked with the town's great temples, Indreshwar Mahadev and Brahmayani, and with the twelve-yearly Makar Mela, when pilgrims come from across Nepal to bathe here. Its quiet setting, between fields and old houses, makes it one of the most peaceful riverside sacred sites in the region.

loreChunks.title: Steps, Shrines and Rest Houses
loreChunks.text: The ghat consists of stone steps descending to the water at the confluence, with small shrines, lingams and images set along the banks. Rest houses, known as patis and sattals, provide shelter for pilgrims and for families attending cremations, which take place on platforms by the river. The ensemble is modest in scale but harmonious, with brick and stone structures stepping down toward the water and the roofs of Panauti's old town visible beyond. Bridges and paths connect the ghat with the Brahmayani temple and with the town. The riverbanks change with the seasons, as monsoon floods raise the water and sometimes damage the steps and shrines. Field collectors are asked to document the ghat's structures, shrines and inscriptions, mapping them in relation to the confluence and the town's temples so that the whole sacred landscape can be understood together.

loreChunks.title: The Invisible River
loreChunks.text: The idea of an invisible third river echoes the famous confluence at Prayag in India, where the Ganga and Yamuna are said to meet the hidden Saraswati. At Panauti, the invisible Lilavati completes the sacred triad, and local legends tell stories of its origin, sometimes linked with a woman or goddess who became a river. Bathing at a tribeni is believed to bring great merit and purification, washing away sins and supporting liberation. The lingams and images along the banks honour Shiva and other deities associated with water and with death and transformation. Cremation at the confluence, like cremation at Pashupati, is considered auspicious. The ghat's iconography is thus less about individual images than about the sacred landscape itself, in which water, stone and ritual combine. For visitors, it offers a quieter introduction to the meanings that rivers carry in Hindu thought.

loreChunks.title: Makar Mela and Everyday Rites
loreChunks.text: Every twelve years, Tribeni Ghat hosts the Makar Mela, a great bathing festival in the month of Magh, when the sun enters Capricorn and pilgrims from across Nepal and beyond come to bathe in the confluence over several weeks. The festival transforms the quiet town, filling it with pilgrims, sadhus, stalls and music. In other years, the ghat is the setting for everyday rites: morning bathing, offerings at the riverside shrines, rituals for the dead and cremations. During the annual Panauti Jatra, the town's deities are associated with the confluence and its ghats. Visitors are welcome to walk along the ghat and observe, but should behave respectfully, avoid photographing cremations or mourners, and dress modestly. A local guide or homestay host can explain the festivals and the legends of the invisible river, and suggest the best times to visit.

loreChunks.title: Floods and Fragile Banks
loreChunks.text: The ghat's riverside location exposes it to monsoon floods, which can erode the banks, damage steps and undermine shrines. Changes in river flow caused by upstream development, sand mining and changes in land use add to these pressures, and pollution threatens the water's quality for ritual bathing. The 1988 and 2015 earthquakes affected buildings in Panauti, including structures near the ghat, and repairs were carried out by the community and local authorities. Panauti's community-based tourism and heritage initiatives help to raise awareness and funds for conservation. Protecting the confluence requires attention to the rivers as well as to the built structures, linking heritage conservation with environmental management. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the ghat in both dry and monsoon seasons where possible, recording changes to the banks and structures, and to map its shrines systematically.

audioHook.script: Walk down the stone steps to the water, where two rivers meet below the old town of Panauti. Locals will tell you there is a third river here too, the Lilavati, which no one can see. A meeting of three rivers is called a tribeni, and bathing at one is believed to wash away a lifetime of sins. Every twelve years, the quiet ghat explodes with life during the Makar Mela, when pilgrims and sadhus arrive from across Nepal to bathe here for weeks. On ordinary days you may see morning bathers, offerings at the little riverside shrines and, sometimes, a cremation, so move gently and keep your camera away from mourners. Who was the invisible river before she became water? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Panauti guide tell you her story.
